title: Evaluation — FID, CLIP Score, Human Preference

questions.question: A generative benchmark needs to measure both output realism and prompt matching. Why use more than one metric?
options: Human preference and embeddings always disagree
FID and CLIP use the same feature distribution
Quality and conditioning adherence are different axes
A single metric cannot be computed on images
questions.explanation: FID compares real and generated feature distributions as a sample-quality measure, while CLIP score compares image and prompt embeddings for adherence. These are different axes, so one cannot stand in for both.

questions.question: How should FID change when generated and real feature distributions become more similar?
options: FID should decrease
FID should equal CLIP score
FID should increase
FID should become a percentage
questions.explanation: FID is a Fréchet distance between Gaussian fits to real and generated Inception features; more similar distributions have smaller distance. Thus a better match lowers FID rather than raising it.

questions.question: What does CLIP score compute for one generated image and prompt?
options: Pixelwise MSE between image and prompt tokens
A human pairwise preference and Elo rating
Cosine similarity of image and text embeddings
Fréchet distance between two Inception Gaussians
questions.explanation: CLIP score is the cosine similarity between the generated image’s CLIP embedding and the prompt’s CLIP text embedding. FID uses distribution-level Inception features, and Elo aggregates pairwise preference outcomes.

questions.question: A team reports FID from 1,000 generated samples. Which concern follows the lesson’s evaluation guidance?
options: The score directly reflects human preferences
It no longer depends on Inception features
Small-sample covariance estimates make it unreliable
It now measures prompt adherence instead of quality
questions.explanation: With only 1,000 samples, estimated feature covariances can be biased; the lesson recommends at least 10,000 for FID. The issue is reliability of the distribution estimate, not a change to what FID measures.

questions.question: A CLIP score rises after adding “masterpiece, 4k, high quality” to every prompt, but visual binding is unchanged. What likely happened?
options: The Inception feature extractor changed domains
FID was converted into a human Elo score
The model necessarily improved compositional reasoning
The score was gamed by prompt wording
questions.explanation: CLIP can reward prompt phrases such as “masterpiece” or “4k” even when the actual image-text binding is unchanged, inflating the metric through wording. Keep prompts consistent and inspect outputs to detect this gaming.

questions.question: A release report must support a claim that the new model improved overall. What evaluation bundle does the lesson recommend?
options: FID alone on one convenient prompt set, without human review
One human rating on the best generated sample from each model
FID, CLIP adherence, blinded preference, and failure review
CLIP score alone with hand-picked prompts and no visual audit
questions.explanation: A defensible overall comparison combines distribution quality (FID), prompt adherence (CLIP or related scores), blinded preference, and qualitative failure analysis. One metric or one cherry-picked sample can hide a distinct failure mode.
